articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $4.2M consulting contract bypassed normal bidding. Commissioners say they didn't know.
articles.dek: Public records show the contract was split into smaller chunks to avoid competitive procurement thresholds. Three commissioners now claim they were unaware of the arrangement.
brief: A $4.2 million consulting contract with Atlanta-based Meridian Strategic Group was divided into 23 separate purchase orders over 18 months, keeping each below the $200,000 threshold requiring competitive bidding
Three of five Escambia County commissioners say they were unaware of the cumulative spending until a Flightline public records request revealed the pattern
County Administrator Wes Moreno defended the arrangement as 'operationally efficient' while the county attorney's office reviews whether procurement policies were violated
articles.body:
The invoices arrived every three to five weeks. Sometimes $187,000. Sometimes $162,000. Once, $199,400—six hundred dollars under the limit that would have required Escambia County to open the work to competitive bids.

Over 18 months, from January 2025 through last month, Meridian Strategic Group of Atlanta billed Escambia County $4.2 million for what county documents describe as "organizational assessment," "operational efficiency analysis" and "strategic implementation support." The money came from the general fund. No single payment triggered the county's $200,000 competitive procurement threshold.

The Flightline obtained 847 pages of invoices, purchase orders and internal emails through a public records request submitted in May. The documents show a pattern: 23 separate purchase orders, each authorized at the department level, each just under the ceiling that would have sent the contract to the Board of County Commissioners for approval.

Three commissioners say they had no idea.

"News to me"

Commissioner Lumon May was sitting in his district office on Navy Boulevard when a reporter read him the total figure.

"Four point two million," he repeated. "For consulting." He leaned back in his chair. "That's news to me."

May, who represents District 3, said he recalled approving what he believed was a one-time $180,000 contract with Meridian in early 2025 for a "departmental workflow study." He was unaware of subsequent payments.

"If you're telling me we've spent four million dollars with one company and I never voted on it, then something's broken in this process," May said. "Either I wasn't paying attention or I wasn't given the opportunity to pay attention. Neither one of those is acceptable."

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, District 1, said he learned of the cumulative spending two weeks ago when contacted by The Flightline. In an email, he called the arrangement "concerning" and said he had requested a full accounting from the county administrator's office.

"I don't like surprises," Bergosh wrote. "Especially not $4 million surprises."

Commissioner Mike Kohler, District 4, did not respond to three interview requests. His office sent a two-sentence statement: "Commissioner Kohler supports fiscal responsibility and proper procurement procedures. He looks forward to reviewing the matter."

The remaining two commissioners—Chair Steven Barry and Vice Chair Doug Underhill—declined to say whether they knew of the cumulative spending before it became public. Through a spokesperson, both said they would wait for the county attorney's review before commenting.

How purchase orders work

Escambia County's procurement policy, last updated in 2019, establishes clear thresholds. Purchases under $50,000 require only department head approval. Those between $50,000 and $200,000 need additional sign-off from the county administrator. Anything over $200,000 must go through competitive bidding and requires a commission vote.

The policy includes a specific prohibition: "Splitting or structuring purchases to avoid procurement thresholds is prohibited."

The Meridian invoices tell a different story.

A January 2025 purchase order for $194,000 covered "Phase 1 assessment." A February 2025 order for $188,000 covered "Phase 1 implementation support." A March order for $176,500 covered "Phase 2 assessment." The pattern continued through June 2026.

Internal emails show some county staff noticed. In April 2025, a budget analyst in the Office of Management and Budget wrote to her supervisor: "This is the fifth Meridian PO this quarter. Cumulative is now over $800K. Should this be going to procurement?"

The supervisor's response, three hours later: "Administrator's office is aware. Process as submitted."

County Administrator Wes Moreno, in a written statement provided through the county's communications office, said the purchase orders were "processed in accordance with established procedures."

"Each engagement with Meridian addressed distinct operational needs," Moreno wrote. "The work products were delivered on schedule and have contributed to meaningful improvements in county operations. We are confident that all applicable policies were followed."

Asked specifically whether splitting the contract into smaller pieces to avoid competitive bidding violated county policy, Moreno did not respond.

Who is Meridian?

Meridian Strategic Group operates from a single office in Atlanta's Buckhead district. Georgia corporate records list the company as an LLC formed in 2018. Its registered agent is a corporate services firm that handles filings for hundreds of Georgia businesses.

The company has no website. It has no LinkedIn presence. It does not appear in any searchable database of government contractors maintained by the state of Florida or the federal government.

The Flightline contacted Meridian through the phone number listed on its invoices to Escambia County. A woman who answered identified herself as "client services" and took a message. No one returned the call.

The invoices themselves provide limited detail. Each lists the same Atlanta address, the same federal tax identification number and a brief description of services. None include itemized hours, personnel names or specific deliverables.

A March 2025 invoice for $185,000, for example, describes the work as: "Continued assessment and implementation support services per engagement agreement." A November 2025 invoice for $191,000 says only: "Strategic consultation and operational guidance—Q4 activities."

Asked what specific work products the county received for $4.2 million, Moreno's office provided a three-page summary listing 11 "workstreams," including "organizational structure optimization," "technology systems evaluation" and "community engagement framework development."

The summary does not include any reports, presentations or other tangible deliverables. When The Flightline requested copies of all documents produced by Meridian, the county's records custodian said the search was ongoing and would require an additional 30 days.

The legal question

Florida law gives counties broad discretion in procurement, but it does not permit circumventing competitive bidding requirements through contract splitting.

A 2014 Florida Attorney General opinion addressed a similar situation in Volusia County, where a series of small contracts with a single vendor triggered concerns about bid avoidance. The opinion concluded that "the deliberate structuring of purchases to evade competitive procurement thresholds violates both the letter and spirit" of local purchasing policies.

Escambia County Attorney Alison Rogers said her office is reviewing the Meridian payments. She declined to characterize the arrangement or predict any outcome.

"We've been asked to look at it, and we're looking at it," Rogers said. "I'm not going to prejudge anything."

Rogers said the review would examine whether the payments constituted a single contract that should have been competitively bid, or whether they represented legitimately separate engagements that happened to involve the same vendor.

"That distinction matters," she said. "And it's fact-dependent."

The review has no public deadline. Rogers said she would present findings to the commission "when we have something to present."

What happens next

Commissioner May said he plans to request a formal agenda item at the commission's August 7 meeting to discuss the Meridian contract and the county's procurement oversight procedures.

"Four million dollars bought us something," May said. "I want to see it. I want to know what we got. And I want to understand how this happened without anyone on this board being asked to weigh in."

He paused. "We approve roadwork contracts. We approve park maintenance contracts. We debate for an hour over $50,000 for a community nonprofit. But four million dollars to a consulting firm nobody's heard of just... slides through?"

May said he was not accusing anyone of wrongdoing. He said he wanted answers.

"Maybe there's a perfectly good explanation," he said. "I'd love to hear it."

Bergosh, in a follow-up email, said he shared May's concerns. He also raised a question about the county administrator's role.

"The board hired Wes to run day-to-day operations," Bergosh wrote. "We trust his judgment. But part of that trust is keeping us informed when spending reaches this level with a single vendor. If the process allowed this to happen without board awareness, the process needs to change. And we need to understand why it wasn't flagged."

Moreno's statement did not address whether he believed the commission should have been informed of the cumulative spending.

The invoices

The Flightline is publishing the complete set of Meridian invoices and purchase orders obtained through public records. The documents total 847 pages.

They show spending by month, from $162,000 in February 2025 to a peak of $287,000 in October 2025—the only month when payments exceeded $200,000, though that total was split across two separate purchase orders dated eight days apart.

They show approval signatures from three different department heads in the county administrator's office, each authorizing payments for work described in nearly identical language.

They show, in one April 2025 email chain, a discussion among budget staff about whether to flag the cumulative spending for senior leadership. The chain ends with a note from a supervisor: "Already discussed with WM. No further action needed."

WM are the initials of Wes Moreno.

This story will be updated as the county attorney's review progresses. The Flightline has submitted additional records requests for all communications between county staff and Meridian Strategic Group, as well as any contracts or engagement letters governing the consulting relationship.

articles.label: Development & Infrastructure
articles.headline: The 17-Mile Stretch: Why Pensacola Beach road repairs keep getting pushed back
articles.dek: FDOT has delayed the Via de Luna repaving project three times since 2024. Beach residents and business owners say the patchwork fixes aren't holding through summer traffic.
brief: FDOT has postponed the Via de Luna resurfacing project three times since originally scheduling it for fall 2024
Beach business owners report losing customers who avoid the drive due to road conditions
The project's current timeline places construction during the 2027 tourist season, drawing opposition from the Santa Rosa Island Authority
articles.body:
The pothole appears every three weeks. Same spot. Eastbound Via de Luna, half a mile past the toll plaza, right where the asphalt meets a storm drain grate.

Maria Gonzalez knows because she's the one who keeps calling it in. The owner of Surf & Sand Rentals has watched road crews fill the hole four times since March. Each patch lasts until the next hard rain.

"I had a customer last week who got a flat tire right there," Gonzalez said. "She turned around and went back to the mainland. Rented bikes somewhere else."

The 17-mile stretch of Via de Luna Drive from the Bob Sikes Bridge to the Navarre Beach line was supposed to get a full resurfacing two years ago. The Florida Department of Transportation first scheduled the $14.2 million project for October 2024. Then spring 2025. Then fall 2025. The current timeline shows construction beginning in March 2027.

Three delays. No shovels in the ground. And a road that beach residents say is getting worse by the month.

The funding shuffle

FDOT District Three spokesperson Amanda Chen said the delays stem from what she called "funding prioritization adjustments" at the state level.

"The Via de Luna project remains in our five-year work program," Chen said in an emailed statement. "Construction timelines are subject to revision based on available funding and statewide infrastructure needs."

What Chen did not say: Hurricane costs have eaten into FDOT's resurfacing budget for three consecutive years. The agency spent $847 million on storm repairs statewide in 2025 alone, according to budget documents obtained through a public records request. Routine maintenance projects got pushed back across the Panhandle.

Via de Luna isn't the only delayed road in Escambia County. Cervantes Street, Navy Boulevard and sections of Mobile Highway have all seen resurfacing timelines extended. But Via de Luna carries a particular burden. The road serves as the only vehicular route onto Santa Rosa Island west of Navarre. Every tourist, every delivery truck, every emergency vehicle uses the same two lanes.

Escambia County traffic data shows Via de Luna averaged 18,400 vehicles per day during June 2026. On the Saturday of Memorial Day weekend, the count hit 31,000.

Patches on patches

The current road surface dates to 2011. FDOT designed it for a 15-year lifespan. That window closed last year.

What's left is a patchwork. Driving the full stretch from the toll plaza to Portofino reveals the history: dark gray patches from 2023, lighter ones from last winter, fresh black tar from repairs done in May. The mismatched sections create an uneven surface that shudders under tires.

Tom Bradley has driven the road daily for 22 years. He owns a house on Ariola Drive and commutes to his accounting firm in downtown Pensacola. He said the road has never been this rough.

"Used to be you'd hit a bad spot here and there," Bradley said. "Now it's like driving on a washboard for three miles straight through the residential section."

The worst segments cluster between the main public beach access points, where heavy traffic combines with underground utility work from the ongoing sewer expansion project. Santa Rosa Island Authority maintenance director James Polk said the utility cuts have created weak points that fail faster than the surrounding pavement.

"Every time you cut into a road and patch it, you create a seam," Polk said. "Water gets in. It freezes in winter, expands. The patch pops out. We're chasing the same failures over and over."

SRIA crews filled 847 potholes on Via de Luna between January and June of this year. The authority spent $124,000 on patching materials alone—money that comes from the beach's parking revenue and toll collections.

The business impact

Pensacola Beach business owners started a petition last month asking FDOT to accelerate the project timeline. The document, submitted to District Three headquarters in Chipley on July 1, carried 156 signatures.

The petition argues that road conditions are actively harming the beach economy. Several business owners said customers have complained about the drive.

"People come down here expecting paradise," said Rick Abernathy, general manager of the Hampton Inn on Via de Luna. "They don't expect to feel like they're driving through a construction zone for 20 minutes just to get to their hotel."

Abernathy said his front desk staff fields questions about the road weekly. Some guests have asked whether there's an alternate route. There isn't.

The Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce declined to take an official position on the petition but acknowledged member concerns. Executive Director Alison Westbrook said the chamber has communicated with FDOT about the timeline.

"We understand there are budget realities," Westbrook said. "We're just asking for clarity on when this is actually going to happen."

A 2027 problem

The current FDOT schedule creates a new concern for beach stakeholders. If construction begins in March 2027 as planned, work would extend into the summer tourist season.

Chen, the FDOT spokesperson, said the agency "makes every effort to minimize impacts to local businesses during construction." She said typical resurfacing projects on similar roads take four to six months.

Do the math. A March start with a six-month timeline means crews working through August—the peak of beach season.

SRIA board member Patricia Salazar raised the timing issue at the authority's June meeting. She asked staff to formally request that FDOT either accelerate the project to finish before Memorial Day 2027 or delay it until fall.

"We cannot have lane closures on Via de Luna in July," Salazar said. "That's not an inconvenience. That's an economic catastrophe for this island."

The board voted unanimously to send a letter to FDOT. As of press time, the authority had not received a response.

What happens next

FDOT's five-year work program undergoes annual revision each July. The 2027 update, expected later this month, will determine whether Via de Luna's timeline shifts again.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said he plans to lobby FDOT leadership to prioritize the project. He called the current timeline "unacceptable."

"This isn't some back road," Bergosh said. "This is the main artery to one of the top tourist destinations in Northwest Florida. We're talking about tens of millions of dollars in economic impact every year, and we can't keep the road drivable."

For now, the patches continue. SRIA has a crew scheduled to fill holes on the eastern stretch of Via de Luna this Thursday. Polk expects they'll be back at the same spots within a month.

The pothole near the storm drain grate—the one Maria Gonzalez keeps calling about—got filled again last Tuesday. She drove past it this morning.

"Already cracking," she said. "Give it two weeks."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's pilot training backlog hits 18 months. Student aviators are waiting tables to pay rent.
articles.dek: A shortage of instructors and aircraft has left hundreds of student naval aviators in limbo. Some have been in Pensacola for two years without completing primary training.
brief: Student naval aviators at NAS Pensacola face average waits of 18 months before starting primary flight training, with some waiting over two years
The backlog stems from instructor shortages and aging T-6B Texan II aircraft availability, according to Navy officials and student pilots
Dozens of student aviators have taken part-time jobs in restaurants and retail to supplement their basic officer pay while stuck in administrative limbo
articles.body:
The lunch rush at McGuire's Irish Pub on a Wednesday in June. A server in a green polo weaves between tables of tourists, balancing plates of corned beef and shepherd's pie. His name tag says Tyler. His military ID says Ensign Tyler Rawlings, United States Navy.

Rawlings, 24, graduated from the Naval Academy in May 2024. He reported to NAS Pensacola that July expecting to earn his wings within 18 months. Thirteen months later, he's still waiting to begin primary flight training.

"I serve beer to people who ask what I do, and I tell them I'm a pilot," Rawlings said during a break between shifts. "Then they ask what I fly, and I have to explain that I don't fly anything. Not yet."

He's not alone. According to figures provided by Naval Air Training Command, 847 student naval aviators are currently assigned to NAS Pensacola and NAS Whiting Field awaiting primary flight training. The average wait time has stretched to 18.3 months—up from 11 months in 2023 and just 4 months a decade ago.

The bottleneck has created an unusual scene across Pensacola: young officers with college degrees and security clearances working as bartenders, delivery drivers and retail clerks. Not because they washed out. Because there aren't enough instructors or aircraft to train them.

'Awaiting Training' Is Still a Job

Student naval aviators in the training pipeline hold the official status of "awaiting training," or ATWT. They report to the base daily. They attend ground school. They maintain physical fitness standards. They're subject to the Uniform Code of Military Justice.

What they don't do is fly.

"The Navy owns you 24/7," said Lt. Cmdr. Marcus Chen, a spokesman for Naval Air Training Command. "These are commissioned officers on active duty. They're being paid, they're serving, they're just in a holding pattern due to capacity constraints."

That pay—roughly $3,800 per month for an ensign with less than two years of service—covers the basics in most cities. In Pensacola's post-pandemic rental market, it doesn't go far.

Average rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the Pensacola metro area hit $1,340 in June 2026, according to Zillow data. Add car payments, insurance, student loans from pre-commissioning programs, and the math gets tight.

The Navy provides no additional housing allowance for unmarried junior officers in the Pensacola area. Those who live off-base—most do, as on-base housing is limited—absorb the full cost.

"I'm not complaining about my situation," said Ensign Maria Santos, 23, an Aviation Preflight Indoctrination student who picks up weekend shifts at a downtown boutique. "I signed up for this. But when you tell people you're a military officer working retail, they look at you funny."

What Caused the Backlog

The pilot training crunch has multiple causes, none of them new. What's new is how they've converged.

Instructor availability is the primary constraint. Naval aviators who complete their fleet tours and return to Pensacola as instructors are in short supply. Commercial airlines, recovering from their own pilot shortage, have been offering six-figure signing bonuses to military pilots willing to separate. The Navy has responded with retention bonuses of its own, but the competition has thinned the instructor pipeline.

Aircraft availability is the secondary constraint. The T-6B Texan II, the primary training aircraft for both Navy and Air Force student pilots, has an aging airframe. Depot-level maintenance takes aircraft out of rotation for months at a time. A 2024 Government Accountability Office report found the T-6B fleet operating at 67% of required capacity.

Then there's simple volume. Navy recruiting exceeded targets in 2023 and 2024 after several down years. More accessions meant more officers feeding into a training pipeline that hadn't expanded to match.

"You can't just stand up more instructor billets overnight," Chen said. "These are experienced aviators with specific qualifications. The capacity exists, but expanding it takes years."

Chief of Naval Air Training Rear Adm. Robert Westbrook acknowledged the backlog at a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing in March, calling it "a readiness challenge we're addressing with urgency." He cited plans to expand simulator capacity and cross-train Coast Guard helicopter pilots as supplemental instructors.

Those measures won't produce results until 2027 at the earliest, according to Navy projections.

Two Years and Counting

The longest-waiting student aviators at NAS Pensacola have been in the city since early 2024. Some arrived expecting to spend 18 months in Pensacola total. They've now exceeded that just waiting to start.

Lt. j.g. Devon Park, 26, reported to Pensacola in February 2024 after completing Officer Candidate School. He began primary flight training in January 2026—a 23-month wait. He expects to complete it by September, at which point he'll move to advanced training in Corpus Christi or Meridian.

"I'll have been in uniform almost three years before I earn my wings," Park said. "Guys who went through 10 years ago were done in 18 months total."

The extended timeline affects more than schedules. Promotion timelines, career progression, and retirement calculations all assume a standard training pipeline. Officers who spend two years ATWT don't get that time credited differently.

"You're not behind your peers on paper," Park said. "But you feel behind. You're watching people you went to OCS with get to the fleet while you're still here."

The Pensacola Economy, Inadvertently

The student aviator population has become an accidental fixture of Pensacola's service economy. Restaurant managers, familiar with the pattern, have learned to recruit from the ATWT pool. The workers are reliable, educated and available for odd shifts. They also leave without notice when training slots open.

"We probably have six or seven at any given time," said Danny Kowalski, general manager at a sports bar near the base. "Good kids. They're upfront about their situation. I know they're gone the moment they get a flight date."

The arrangement is permitted under Defense Department regulations, which allow servicemembers to hold off-duty employment provided it doesn't interfere with military duties or create conflicts of interest. Student aviators must submit requests to their commanding officers, who approve or deny based on scheduling conflicts.

Most requests are approved. There's not much else for ATWT students to do.

"Ground school is maybe two hours a day," said one student aviator who asked not to be named because he hadn't cleared his comments with public affairs. "PT in the morning. Then you're just waiting. You can only study so much. You can only work out so much."

Some students use the time productively. Several have completed graduate degrees through online programs. Others have earned civilian flight certifications on their own dime, though those hours don't count toward Navy requirements.

Many just wait.

What Comes Next

Navy officials insist the backlog will ease. New instructor retention incentives take effect in October. A contract for additional T-6B depot maintenance capacity was signed in April. The planned introduction of a new advanced trainer, the T-7A Red Hawk, is expected to push more advanced training capacity to other bases, freeing instructor bandwidth at Pensacola.

Student aviators have heard these projections before.

"They told us the same thing last year," Rawlings said. "I'm not pessimistic. I'm just realistic. I'll fly when they tell me I fly."

Until then, he has a shift at McGuire's on Thursday night. Tips are good when the Blue Angels are in town.
